name: Jerusalem
nameChange: Sometimes called Salem in the patriarchal narratives; under Roman rule (135 AD) rebuilt as Aelia Capitolina before its ancient name returned.
significance: Capital of ancient Israel and site of the Temple — the spiritual center of biblical history.

name: Bethlehem
nameChange: The older patriarchal name Ephrath survives in Genesis and Micah; the name Bethlehem ('house of bread') has remained constant.
significance: Birthplace of King David and of Jesus; Rachel was buried on the road nearby.

name: Nazareth
nameChange: An obscure village in the first century — 'can any good thing come out of Nazareth?' — now a major city of northern Israel.
significance: The Galilean town where Jesus grew up and where the angel Gabriel announced his coming to Mary.

name: Jericho
nameChange: The Arabic Ariha preserves the Hebrew name; one of the oldest continuously inhabited towns on earth.
significance: Walled city whose defeat opened Israel's conquest of Canaan; later setting for Zacchaeus and blind Bartimaeus.

name: Hebron
nameChange: Genesis calls it Kiriath-Arba; the Arabic name Al-Khalil ('the Friend') honors Abraham, called the friend of God.
significance: Burial place of the patriarchs in the cave of Machpelah and David's first capital.

name: Mount Sinai
nameChange: The Arabic Jebel Musa means 'Moses's mountain'; the traditional identification with Jebel Musa is ancient but unconfirmed.
significance: The mountain where Moses received the Ten Commandments and Elijah heard the still small voice.

name: Babylon
nameChange: The ancient capital lies in ruins near modern Hillah; once the greatest city of the ancient world, now mounds of brick.
significance: Capital of the empire that exiled Judah; setting of Daniel and the exiled prophets.

name: Egypt
nameChange: Hebrew Mitzrayim and Greek Aigyptos are unrelated names; the ancient Egyptians themselves called their land Kemet.
significance: Land of bondage and refuge — setting of Joseph's rise, the Exodus, and the Holy Family's flight.

name: Damascus
nameChange: Among the oldest continuously inhabited cities on earth; the name has persisted essentially unchanged for four thousand years.
significance: Where Saul was struck blind on the road and converted to follow Christ.

name: Antioch of Syria
nameChange: Founded c. 300 BC by Seleucus I and named for his father Antiochus; the modern Turkish Antakya preserves the ancient name.
significance: The city where the followers of Jesus were first called Christians; the launching point of Paul's missionary journeys.

name: Corinth
nameChange: Sacked by Rome in 146 BC and refounded as a Roman colony in 44 BC; ancient Corinth is now an archaeological site beside the modern city.
significance: Roman trading city where Paul founded a major church and wrote letters back.

name: Rome
nameChange: The imperial capital; the name has persisted unchanged from antiquity.
significance: Imperial capital and final destination of Paul's missionary journey; place of his and Peter's traditional martyrdom.

name: Ur of the Chaldees
nameChange: The Sumerian moon-cult city was abandoned by the 4th century BC; rediscovered by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s.
significance: Ancient Sumerian city — the birthplace of Abraham and Lot.

name: The Jordan River
nameChange: The river drops nearly 700 meters from Mount Hermon to the Dead Sea; the Hebrew name 'descender' fits its course.
significance: River where Israel crossed into the promised land, where Elijah was taken up, and where Jesus was baptized.

name: Sea of Galilee
hebrewOrGreekName: יָם כִּנֶּרֶת · ἡ θάλασσα τῆς Γαλιλαίας
nameChange: Bears four names in scripture — Chinnereth in the Hebrew Bible (after its harp shape), Gennesaret in Luke, and Tiberias and Galilee in the Gospels.
significance: The lake whose shores witnessed much of Jesus's teaching and miracles.

name: Capernaum
nameChange: Destroyed in the 8th century AD; the synagogue stones and the traditional house of Peter remain visible in the archaeological park.
significance: Jesus's adopted headquarters on the Sea of Galilee; site of Peter's house, the synagogue, and many miracles.

name: Bethany
nameChange: The modern Arabic name Al-Eizariya derives from 'Lazarus' — preserving the memory of his raising in the very name of the town.
significance: Home of Martha, Mary, and Lazarus; Jesus's frequent resting place outside Jerusalem; site of Lazarus's raising and the ascension nearby.

name: Philippi
nameChange: Renamed by Philip II of Macedon in 356 BC after he captured the gold-rich town of Krenides; refounded as a Roman colony after the battle of Philippi in 42 BC.
significance: First European city where Paul preached; Lydia's conversion; Paul and Silas in prison; later recipient of one of Paul's letters.

name: Thessalonica
nameChange: Founded in 315 BC by Cassander and named for his wife Thessalonike, half-sister of Alexander the Great; the name has persisted with minor spelling change.
significance: Macedonian capital where Paul reasoned in the synagogue for three Sabbaths; recipient of two of his earliest letters.

name: Athens
nameChange: Named for the goddess Athena, patroness of the city; the Greek name has persisted unchanged since antiquity.
significance: Site of Paul's sermon on Mars Hill (the Areopagus) and his disputation with the Stoics and Epicureans at the altar to an unknown god.

name: Ephesus
nameChange: The ancient harbor silted up by the 7th century AD and the city was abandoned; the modern town of Selçuk grew up nearby.
significance: Site of the great Temple of Artemis; Paul's two-year ministry in the hall of Tyrannus; the riot of the silversmiths; later residence of the Apostle John and Mary.

name: Caesarea Maritima
nameChange: Built by Herod the Great between 22 and 10 BC as a deep-water harbor and named for Caesar Augustus; Roman administrative capital of Judea until 70 AD.
significance: Cornelius's conversion opened the gospel to the Gentiles here; Paul's two-year imprisonment under Felix and Festus.

name: Caesarea Philippi
nameChange: The Greek name Paneas (Arabic Banias) recalls a sanctuary of Pan at the springs of the Jordan; rebuilt and renamed by Herod Philip in honor of Caesar around 2 BC.
significance: At the rock of Pan beneath Mount Hermon, Peter confessed Jesus as the Christ — 'on this rock I will build my church.'

name: Nineveh
nameChange: Destroyed in 612 BC by Medes and Babylonians; the ruins (Tell Kuyunjik and Tell Nebi Yunus) now lie across the Tigris from modern Mosul.
significance: Capital of the Assyrian Empire; the great city Jonah was sent to and Nahum prophesied against.

name: Susa
nameChange: The modern town of Shush preserves the ancient name; the citadel mound where Esther moved through the harem is still visible.
significance: Persian capital where Esther became queen, where Daniel saw the visions of the ram and the goat, and where Nehemiah served as cupbearer.

name: Beersheba
ancientName: Beer Sheva ('well of seven' or 'well of the oath')
nameChange: The name preserves Abraham's covenant with Abimelech sealed with seven ewe lambs; the Hebrew dual meaning is built into the place itself.
significance: Southern boundary of Israel ('from Dan to Beersheba'); patriarchal wells; where Hagar found water for Ishmael; where Elijah fled from Jezebel.

name: Shiloh
nameChange: Destroyed by the Philistines after the loss of the ark (c. 1050 BC); the archaeological tell preserves the ancient name in its Arabic form.
significance: Site of the tabernacle for nearly four centuries before David's conquest of Jerusalem; Eli's priesthood, Samuel's call, the resting place of the ark.

name: Samaria
nameChange: Rebuilt by Herod the Great as Sebaste (Greek for 'Augustus'); the modern Arabic village name Sebastia preserves Herod's renaming.
significance: Capital of the northern kingdom of Israel under Omri and Ahab; site of Elisha's later ministry and Philip's evangelistic mission.

name: Megiddo
nameChange: The mound conceals twenty-six layers of occupation from the Neolithic through the Persian period; Hebrew Har-Megiddo ('mount Megiddo') became the Greek Armageddon of Revelation.
significance: Strategic fortress overlooking the Jezreel Valley; Solomon's chariot city; site of Josiah's death; the apocalyptic Armageddon of John's vision.

name: Kadesh Barnea
nameChange: The largest oasis in the Sinai-Negev region; the Arabic name Ain el-Qudeirat preserves the Hebrew root for 'Kadesh.'
significance: Oasis from which the twelve spies were sent into Canaan; the people's refusal cost forty years of wandering; Miriam was buried here.

name: Mount Carmel
nameChange: The forested ridge runs along the Mediterranean coast at modern Haifa; the Hebrew name carries the meaning 'vineyard.'
significance: Coastal mountain where Elijah confronted the four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and fire fell from heaven.

name: Mount Tabor
nameChange: The distinctive dome-shaped peak rises 575 meters above the surrounding Jezreel Valley; the name has remained constant since antiquity.
significance: Where Barak mustered the tribes against Sisera at Deborah's word; the traditional site of the Transfiguration.

name: Shechem
nameChange: The Roman city Neapolis ('new city') was built nearby in 72 AD; the modern Arabic name Nablus derives from Neapolis.
significance: Abraham's first altar in Canaan; Jacob bought land here; Joshua renewed the covenant in the gathering of all Israel; Jesus's conversation with the Samaritan woman at Jacob's well.

name: Joppa
nameChange: Now the southern district of Tel Aviv-Yafo; one of the oldest functioning ports in the world, mentioned in Egyptian records from the fifteenth century BC.
significance: Ancient Mediterranean port; Jonah boarded ship for Tarshish here; Peter raised Tabitha and received the rooftop vision before going to Cornelius.

name: Bethsaida
nameChange: Rebuilt by Herod Philip as Julias in honor of the daughter of Augustus; abandoned in late antiquity; archaeological identification is debated between et-Tell and el-Araj.
significance: Hometown of Peter, Andrew, and Philip; site of the feeding of the five thousand on the eastern shore of the lake.

name: Patmos
significance: The small volcanic island in the Aegean Sea where the apostle John was exiled under Roman persecution and received the visions recorded in the Book of Revelation. The Cave of the Apocalypse, a pilgrimage site since antiquity, marks the traditional location of his revelatory experience. Patmos remains one of the few biblical sites whose identification has never been seriously disputed.

name: Pergamon
significance: One of the seven churches of Revelation and the site of a great acropolis crowned by a temple to Zeus — what Christ calls 'the throne of Satan.' Pergamon was also home to a famous library of 200,000 scrolls and a renowned center of the imperial cult. The church there was praised for holding fast to Christ's name even where the altar to the emperor dominated the skyline.

name: Sardis
significance: Once the glittering capital of the Lydian empire and the city of King Croesus, whose name became synonymous with wealth. By the time of Revelation, Sardis housed a church Christ described as having a reputation for being alive while actually dead — a community resting on former glory. A small remnant was commended for not soiling their garments.

name: Philadelphia (Asia Minor)
significance: One of the seven churches of Revelation and one of only two that receive no rebuke from Christ. Founded by Attalus II of Pergamon and named for his loyalty to his brother, the city sat at the gateway to the central plateau of Asia Minor. Christ's letter promises an open door no one can shut and names this church as those who have kept his word with little strength.

name: Laodicea
significance: The seventh and final church addressed in Revelation, famously rebuked for being neither hot nor cold but lukewarm — a metaphor drawn from the city's own problem of tepid aqueduct water arriving neither as healing hot springs nor refreshing cold. Laodicea was one of the wealthiest cities of Asia Minor, a banking center that boasted it needed nothing; Christ says it is wretched, poor, blind, and naked.

name: Thyatira
significance: One of the seven churches of Revelation and the home city of Lydia, the purple-cloth seller whose conversion in Philippi is described in Acts. The church at Thyatira was praised for love, faith, service, and endurance, but rebuked for tolerating a prophetess Christ calls 'Jezebel' who led believers into sexual immorality and food sacrificed to idols.

name: Smyrna
significance: One of the seven churches of Revelation and one of only two receiving no rebuke. A prosperous port city, Smyrna was a center of the imperial cult and home to a significant Jewish population hostile to the fledgling Christian community. Christ's letter acknowledges their poverty and tribulation, promises that they are rich, and warns of coming persecution — urging them to be faithful unto death in exchange for the crown of life.

name: Ai
significance: The second Canaanite city targeted by Israel after Jericho, whose first assault ended in catastrophic defeat because of Achan's hidden sin. After Achan's judgment, Joshua executed a successful ambush and destroyed the city, a narrative that established the principle that covenant faithfulness, not military strength, determined Israel's victories.

name: Penuel / Peniel
significance: The ford of the Jabbok River where Jacob wrestled through the night with a mysterious divine being and, though his hip was wrenched, refused to let go until he received a blessing. He named the place Peniel — 'face of God' — saying he had seen God face to face and yet lived, a naming that points to the site's function as a threshold between the human and the divine.

name: Bethel
significance: Called Luz before Jacob renamed it, Bethel — 'house of God' — became one of the most theologically loaded sites in the Hebrew Bible. Here Jacob dreamed of a ladder connecting earth and heaven and received the covenant promises. It later became a rival worship site in the Northern Kingdom, a counterfeit sanctuary that the prophets condemned.

name: Dan (city)
significance: The northernmost city of Israel, giving rise to the expression 'from Dan to Beersheba' as the full extent of the land. Originally called Laish, it was captured by the tribe of Dan and renamed. Jeroboam placed one of his two golden calves here to prevent the Northern Kingdom from making pilgrimage to Jerusalem — a sin Amos and Hosea condemned as spiritual adultery.

name: Hazor
significance: The largest Canaanite city-state in the land, called 'the head of all those kingdoms' in Joshua, and the site of a pivotal battle in which Joshua defeated a coalition of northern kings. Hazor was later fortified by Solomon and served as a major administrative center, before being destroyed by the Assyrians under Tiglath-Pileser III in 732 BC.

name: Lachish
significance: The second most important city of Judah after Jerusalem, fortified as a military stronghold and twice the target of devastating siege. Sennacherib of Assyria captured it in 701 BC — the event is commemorated in detailed stone reliefs on his palace walls in Nineveh. Nebuchadnezzar later destroyed it in 587 BC; the Lachish Letters, discovered there, preserve the desperate correspondence of a garrison in its final days.

name: Cana of Galilee
significance: The site of Jesus's first sign in John's Gospel — the turning of water into wine at a wedding banquet — which John says manifested his glory and led his disciples to believe in him. It was also the home of Nathanael and the site of a second sign: the healing of the royal official's son from a distance.

name: Nain
significance: A small village in Galilee where Jesus encountered a widow's funeral procession and raised her only son from the dead without being asked, moved solely by compassion for her grief. Luke records the witnesses' response as awe and the declaration that a great prophet had arisen. The miracle echoes Elijah's raising of the widow of Zarephath's son, placing Jesus in the prophetic tradition while surpassing it.

name: Emmaus
significance: The destination of two disciples on the day of the resurrection, walking away from Jerusalem in despondency when the risen Jesus joined them unrecognized. He explained the scriptures as they walked, and was finally recognized in the breaking of bread — whereupon he vanished. The Emmaus road has become a paradigm for how Christ is encountered: in the word and in the Eucharist.

name: Petra (Sela)
significance: The rose-red city carved into sandstone cliffs, known in Hebrew as Sela (rock) and in Greek as Petra (also rock). The ancient Edomite stronghold was a target of prophetic judgment in Obadiah and Isaiah. It later became the Nabataean capital — a commercial empire straddling the incense trade routes — and the city Paul visited in Arabia after his Damascus road conversion.

name: Ramah
significance: A Benjaminite town north of Jerusalem associated with the prophet Samuel, who judged Israel, anointed Saul and David, and was buried there. Jeremiah heard the voice of Rachel weeping at Ramah when the exiles were assembled there before deportation to Babylon — a lament Matthew sees fulfilled in the slaughter of the innocents at Herod's command.

name: Mizpah (Benjamin)
significance: A major assembly point in the tribal period where Israel gathered for crisis meetings, including the terrible aftermath of the Gibeah atrocity that nearly wiped out Benjamin. Samuel gathered Israel at Mizpah when they demanded a king, and here Saul was publicly presented as the first monarch. After Jerusalem fell, Mizpah served briefly as the seat of Gedaliah's governorship.

name: Gilgal
significance: The first campsite of Israel after crossing the Jordan into Canaan, where Joshua set up twelve memorial stones from the riverbed and the men of the new generation were circumcised — the reproach of Egypt rolled away (gilgal, 'circle of stones,' puns on the verb meaning to roll). Samuel judged Israel here, Saul was confirmed as king at Gilgal, and Elijah and Elisha passed through it before Elijah's translation.

name: Dothan
significance: The place where Joseph's brothers cast him into a cistern and sold him to Ishmaelite traders heading for Egypt — the act of betrayal that, through God's hidden providence, ultimately saved Jacob's family from famine. Centuries later, the city was the scene of Elisha's prayer that his servant's eyes be opened to see the mountain filled with fiery chariots surrounding the enemy Aramean army.

name: Mount Gerizim
significance: The mountain facing Ebal, from whose slopes Moses commanded Israel to recite the blessings upon entering the land. Gerizim became the sacred mountain of the Samaritans, who built their own temple there in competition with Jerusalem. Jesus's conversation with the Samaritan woman at Jacob's Well touched directly on this rivalry — he declared that true worship would soon be neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.

name: Tyre
significance: The great Phoenician port city whose king Hiram supplied the cedar and craftsmen for Solomon's Temple, and whose legendary wealth and pride became the target of extended prophetic judgment in Ezekiel and Isaiah. Jesus visited the region of Tyre and Sidon where he healed the Syrophoenician woman's daughter, a story about the breadth of his mercy breaking ethnic boundaries.

name: Sidon
significance: The oldest of the great Phoenician cities, north of Tyre on the Lebanese coast, and the home of Jezebel's father Ethbaal, whose daughter brought Baal worship into Israel's royal household. Elijah was sent to a widow of Zarephath near Sidon — beyond the borders of Israel — during the drought, a story Jesus cited to explain why God's mercy extends beyond the expected boundaries.

name: Gaza
significance: One of the five major Philistine cities and the southernmost gateway of the land of Canaan. Gaza is woven into the story of Samson — his exploits, his betrayal by Delilah, and his final act of bringing down the temple of Dagon at the cost of his own life. An angel directed Philip south toward the road from Jerusalem to Gaza, where he encountered and baptized the Ethiopian eunuch, one of the New Testament's most dramatic expansions of the gospel across cultural frontiers.
